unit.title: Manage intellectual property to protect and grow business

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: The board of a Jamaican spice exporter asks its general manager to write an intellectual property (IP) strategy. What should the strategy be built around?
options: The firm's business goals and growth plans
The IP strategies of the largest global brands
Registering every idea that staff ever have
Keeping legal fees as low as they can go

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the purpose of managing IP to grow a business?
options: Filing as many patents as possible each year
Using IP to gain an edge and earn income
Keeping all IP secret from every partner
Treating IP purely as a legal cost to cut

questions.stem: A Kingston software firm wants to know which of its IP drives most of its revenue. What should the manager do first?
options: Rank each item by how long ago it was made
Ask the newest staff which items they like
Link each IP item to the products and income it supports
Count the pages in each registration certificate

questions.stem: A craft brewer in St Ann has a brewing method that rivals cannot work out from the beer, and a new label for its bottles. Which mix of protection fits best?
options: A patent for the label, copyright for the method
Publish the method and register nothing
A trade mark for the method, secrecy for the label
Secrecy for the method, a trade mark for the label

questions.stem: A food technologist invents a preserving method that rivals could work out by examining the products once they are on sale. What is the main argument for patenting it rather than keeping it secret?
options: Secrecy fails once rivals can work it out
A patent lasts forever once it is granted
A patent is always cheaper than secrecy
A patent keeps the method hidden from rivals

questions.stem: A firm will show a new product design at a trade fair in Miami next month. When should it apply to protect the design?
options: After the fair, once buyers have said they like it
Only if a rival copies it at the fair
Before the fair, while the design is still new
Within ten years of the fair taking place

questions.stem: A firm has funds to register its trade mark in only three of its eight export markets. How should it choose the three?
options: By the cheapest registration fees alone
By sales, plans and the risk of copying
By the countries closest to Jamaica
By where the managers prefer to travel

questions.stem: Before investing J$12,000,000 in launching a new brand, what should a manager arrange first?
options: A staff vote on the brand's colours, name and look
A price cut to win market share at launch
A loan for twice the planned launch budget
A search for earlier marks that could block it

questions.stem: A Clarendon engineering firm plans to make a new water pump. Why should it check other firms' patents before production starts?
options: To copy the best features of rival pumps
To get a patent of its own automatically
To avoid infringing another firm's rights
To reduce the GCT it charges on its sales

questions.stem: A manager finds that a competitor's patent on a useful process has expired. What does this usually mean?
options: The competitor keeps it for ten more years
Anyone may now use the process it describes
It may be used only in the competitor's country
The patent renews itself without any fees

questions.stem: A firm licenses its brand to a partner in Barbados and agrees that it will license no one else there and will not sell there itself. What type of licence is this?
options: A non-exclusive licence
A sole licence
An open licence
An exclusive licence

questions.stem: A small firm owns a patent but lacks the money to make the product. It wants regular income and to keep ownership. Which option fits best?
options: License it to a maker for royalties
Assign the patent to the highest bidder
Let the patent lapse to save the fees
Give the design free to a larger rival

questions.stem: Under a licence, a partner will pay an upfront fee of J$2,500,000 plus a royalty of 3% on its sales, which are expected to be J$60,000,000 a year for four years. What is the total expected income from the licence?
Which method values a brand by estimating the royalties the firm would have to pay if it had to license the brand from someone else?
options: The historical cost method
The replacement cost method
The relief-from-royalty method
The share price method

questions.stem: A brand is expected to support sales of J$80,000,000 a year. Similar brands are licensed at a royalty of 4% of sales. Using relief from royalty, how much does owning the brand save each year?
A bank is considering lending to a Jamaican music company against its catalogue of song copyrights. What will the bank most need to see?
options: Its plans to record new songs next year
How many followers its artists have
The cost of its studio equipment
A sound valuation and proof of ownership

questions.stem: A firm pays renewal fees on 30 trade marks. Nine are for products it no longer sells and has no plans to use. What should the IP manager recommend?
options: Renew all 30 marks just to be safe
Register nine new marks to replace them
Review the nine and drop or sell those not needed
Stop renewing every mark to save money

questions.stem: A firm plans to register its trade mark in Jamaica for J$60,000 and in five export markets at J$180,000 each. What is the total budget?
Which measure best shows whether a firm's IP is helping the business grow?
options: The number of pages in its IP policy
The number of staff in its legal team
The hours spent in IP meetings
The share of revenue from protected products

questions.stem: A firm's revenue was J$150,000,000 last year, and J$45,000,000 of it came from products protected by its patents and designs. What percentage came from protected products?
A Montego Bay resort chain finds that a small guesthouse overseas uses a similar name. The chain does not trade in that market and has no plans to. What should management weigh before acting?
options: How strongly the managers feel about the copy
The cost of action against the likely harm
Whether any staff have stayed there
The guesthouse's room rates and reviews

questions.stem: Which practice helps a firm learn early that another party is applying to register a mark like its own?
options: Reading its own annual report
Raising its prices in every market
Using a trade mark watch service
Running a yearly staff survey

questions.stem: After taking legal advice, a firm decides to act against a business that is copying its product. Which outcome often settles the matter fastest and most cheaply?
options: Going straight to a full trial in the courts
A public campaign on social media
Copying the copier's products in return
A negotiated settlement, perhaps a licence

questions.stem: A large manufacturer owns a patented technology that does not fit its main business. Which option could create value from it?
options: License it, sell it or spin it off
Keep it unused to block everyone
Publish it free on the firm's website
Let the patent lapse straight away

questions.stem: An investor is considering buying 30% of a Jamaican app company. Why will she check its IP closely?
options: IP has no effect on a firm's value
Much of the firm's value rests on its IP
Investors must register the IP themselves
IP checks are required by the GCT rules

questions.stem: During due diligence, a buyer finds that the firm's main software was written by a freelancer with no written transfer of rights. Why is this a concern?
options: Freelancers always charge royalties later on
The code must then be made public
The buyer must hire the freelancer
The firm may not own the software it sells

questions.stem: How can a manager encourage staff to come up with, and report, ideas that may become valuable IP?
options: Keep all ideas within senior management
Penalise staff whose ideas do not work out well
Reward useful ideas and make reporting easy
Accept ideas only once a year by letter

questions.stem: Why should IP checks be built into each stage of a product development project?
options: So the project finishes well under its budget
So IP is caught and protected as it arises
So the project team can be made smaller
So marketing can start before the design

questions.stem: Why might a manager study the patents a competitor has applied for in the last three years?
options: To copy the patented products at once
To find out the competitor's staff salaries
To cancel the patents with a letter
To see where the competitor is investing

questions.stem: A firm is licensing its technology to a manufacturer. Which term best protects the firm if the manufacturer sells very little?
options: A minimum yearly royalty
A royalty-free first period
An unlimited sales territory
No duty to report sales

questions.stem: Why should a licence agreement let the owner inspect the licensee's sales records?
options: To learn the names of the licensee's staff
To set the prices the licensee charges
To check that royalties are paid correctly
To avoid paying tax on the royalty income

questions.stem: A firm's brand is well known in several export markets but is registered only in Jamaica. What is the biggest IP risk?
options: Its Jamaican registration may be cancelled
Someone may register the brand there first
It may have to change its name at home
Its GCT rate in Jamaica will be raised

questions.stem: An IP manager is building an IP risk register. Which entry belongs in it?
options: Delivery van insurance is due for renewal
Staff canteen prices are going up
Core software relies on a licence ending next year
The office air conditioning is getting old

questions.stem: Why should a firm keep using its registered trade mark in trade?
options: Frequent use raises the renewal fees
Use is needed only before the mark is registered
Steady use removes the need to renew
A mark left unused for years can be lost

questions.stem: A firm with a strong registered mark for coffee plans to sell mugs and T-shirts under the same name. What should it check first?
options: Whether its registration covers those goods
Whether the price of coffee will rise
Whether staff like the new products
Whether the logo can be made larger

questions.stem: Registering and defending a design will cost J$1,800,000 over five years. Without protection, managers expect copies to cut profit by J$600,000 a year over the same five years. What is the net benefit of protecting the design?
A family firm plans to sell the business in five years. Which IP step will do most to raise its sale value?
options: Avoid recording IP to keep things simple
Register IP and make clear who owns it
Pass IP to the owner's children informally
Stop renewing trade marks to cut costs

questions.stem: An association of straw-craft makers wants a mark showing that goods meet agreed quality standards, which any maker who passes its checks may use. Which kind of mark fits?
options: A domain name
A patent
A certification mark
A trade secret

questions.stem: In a growing firm, who should be accountable for the IP strategy?
options: Each staff member acting alone
The firm's external accountant
The newest recruit in marketing
A named senior manager reporting to the board

questions.stem: A firm sells downloadable training videos online. Which measure best protects this income?
options: Access controls with licensed user accounts
Posting the full videos free on public sites
Removing the copyright notice from them
Emailing the files to anyone who asks

questions.stem: A firm is about to launch a new product name across the Caribbean. Which order of steps is best?
options: Launch, then search
Search, file, then launch
Launch, file, then search
File only if sales are strong

questions.stem: Engineers have made a small improvement that rivals could easily design around and that will be out of date in a year. What is the most sensible approach?
options: Patent it in every export market
Publish full details for all rivals
Record it, but do not pay to patent it
Sue anyone who makes a similar part

questions.stem: How often should a firm review its IP strategy?
options: Only when it is sued
Once, when the firm is founded
Only when a patent expires
At set times and when the business changes

questions.stem: Which items should a quarterly IP report to the board include?
options: Income, costs, risks and coming renewals
Every email about IP sent during that quarter
Staff birthdays and leave dates
The full text of each registration

questions.stem: A Jamaican manufacturer will license a foreign firm's technology. Which term should it negotiate to help its own business grow?
options: A ban on making its own improvements
Rights to the improvements it makes itself
No technical support or staff training
All royalties for 20 years paid in advance

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What three-letter short form names a check of whether a new product can be made and sold without infringing other people's rights?
What one-word term names the outright transfer of ownership of an IP right to another party?
What one-word term names the party that receives permission to use another firm's IP under a licence?
What one-word term describes what happens to a registered IP right when its renewal fee is not paid in time?
A firm spends J$1,500,000 a year managing its IP and earns J$6,000,000 a year from licensing it. How many times does the licensing income cover the cost?
What one-word term names the whole set of IP rights a firm holds and manages together?
What two-word term names the date of a first filing, which an applicant may rely on when filing in other countries within a set time?
What term names a new business set up to develop and sell IP created by a university or a larger firm?
What one-word term names assets, such as IP, that are pledged to a lender as security for a loan?
A firm holds 24 trade mark registrations due for renewal. The renewal cost averages J$45,000 a mark. What is the total renewal cost, in J$?
What two-word term names the careful investigation a buyer or investor makes of a firm, including its IP, before a deal?
What two-word term names the valuation approach that values IP by the future earnings it is expected to bring in?
What two-word term names working with outside partners, such as universities and start-ups, to share ideas and develop new products faster?
What two-word term names an arrangement in which several owners agree to license their related patents together as one package?
A firm spends J$2,400,000 protecting a product design and expects extra profit of J$800,000 a year because rivals cannot copy it. How many years will it take to recover the cost?

essays.stem: A food manufacturer in St Catherine plans to begin exporting to three Caribbean and North American markets within two years. Describe how you would develop an IP strategy to support this growth.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start from the business plan: which products will be exported, to which markets, when, and through which partners. I would then identify the IP that supports those products, such as the brand names and logos, label designs, recipes and processes, and confirm the firm owns them. Next, I would check the risks in each market by searching for earlier trade marks and similar products, so the brand can be used safely. The strategy would set out how each item is protected: trade marks registered in the target markets before launch, label designs protected where copying is likely, and recipes kept as trade secrets with confidentiality agreements for distributors and co-packers. I would set priorities and a budget based on expected sales and the risk of copying, with a timeline that files before any public launch. The strategy would cover licensing or distribution agreements, monitoring for copies, and how infringement will be handled. It would name the senior manager responsible, set measures such as protected export sales and IP costs, and be reviewed each year and whenever markets change.
markingPoints: Starts from business goals and export plans
Identifies IP and confirms ownership
Clearance checks in target markets
Matches protection to each asset, with priorities, budget and timing
Covers agreements, monitoring, responsibility, measures and review

essays.stem: A firm has developed a new process that cuts its production costs by 15%. Evaluate whether it should patent the process or keep it as a trade secret, and make a recommendation.
essays.modelAnswer: A patent would give the firm the right to stop others using the process for a limited period, usually up to about twenty years, even if they develop it on their own. It can be licensed or used to attract investment, and it is a clear asset to show buyers. However, the application costs money, protection is needed in each country of interest, and the process must be described in full and published, so rivals learn from it and may design around it. When the patent ends, anyone may use it. A trade secret costs less, has no time limit and reveals nothing, but it is protected only while it stays secret. It gives no protection if a rival works the process out independently or by examining the product, and it depends on strong controls over staff and partners. The decision depends on whether the process can be detected in the finished product, how long it will stay valuable, and the firm's budget. If the process cannot be seen in the product and the firm can control access, I recommend keeping it secret; if rivals could work it out, a patent is the better choice.
markingPoints: Benefits and limits of a patent, including publication and limited term
Benefits and limits of a trade secret, including loss on discovery
Identifies deciding factors: detectability, lifespan, cost, control
Considers licensing or investment value
Clear recommendation justified by the factors

essays.stem: A young Jamaican firm holds a patent on a solar crop dryer but has little capital. Compare licensing, selling the patent, forming a joint venture and making the product itself, and recommend one option.
essays.modelAnswer: Making the product itself would let the firm keep all the profit and control quality, but it needs factory space, staff and working capital that the firm does not have, so the risk is high. Selling the patent through an assignment would bring a lump sum quickly with little risk, but the firm would give up all future income and control, and might sell for less than the patent is worth. Licensing would let a manufacturer with capital and distribution make and sell the dryer while the firm keeps ownership and earns royalties. The risks are a weak licensee and the cost of monitoring, but these can be managed with minimum royalties, quality standards and audit rights. A joint venture would combine the firm's patent with a partner's money and market access, sharing profit and control, but it is complex to set up, and disagreements can be hard to resolve. Given the firm's lack of capital and its wish to grow, I recommend licensing, perhaps non-exclusively by region, with minimum royalties and the right to take back the licence if targets are missed. This earns income now and keeps the option of making the product later.
markingPoints: Own production: control and profit but high capital need
Sale: quick cash but loss of future income
Licensing: income with ownership kept; controls needed
Joint venture: shared resources, profit and control; complexity
Recommendation justified by the firm's situation

essays.stem: A firm can protect a new product design in its main markets at a cost of J$4,500,000 over five years, and expects extra profit of J$1,500,000 a year from being the only seller. If it does not protect the design, it expects copies within a year and extra profit of only J$400,000 a year over the same five years. Calculate the net five-year result of each option and recommend what the firm should do.
essays.modelAnswer: With protection, the extra profit over five years is 5 × J$1,500,000 = J$7,500,000. Taking away the protection cost of J$4,500,000 leaves a net gain of J$3,000,000. Without protection, there is no protection cost, and the extra profit is 5 × J$400,000 = J$2,000,000. On these figures, protecting the design gives J$1,000,000 more over five years. I would recommend protecting the design, but only after testing the assumptions. The J$1,500,000 a year depends on the protection actually stopping copies, which depends on the firm being willing and able to enforce it in each market. If enforcement is weak, profit may fall towards the unprotected level and the firm would be J$2,500,000 worse off. Managers should check how quickly copies appeared for past products, whether the design will stay popular for five years, and whether costs could be cut by protecting it only in the largest markets. The firm could also license the design in smaller markets to earn extra income. If these checks support the forecast, protection is the better choice.
markingPoints: Protected option: J$7,500,000 less J$4,500,000 = J$3,000,000
Unprotected option: J$2,000,000
Difference of J$1,000,000 in favour of protection
Tests key assumptions, especially enforcement and market life
Justified recommendation, possibly with lower-cost alternatives

essays.stem: A Jamaican cosmetics brand sells across the Caribbean and has a limited legal budget. Describe a practical approach to monitoring its IP and dealing with infringement.
essays.modelAnswer: First, the firm should make sure its marks and designs are registered in its main markets, because enforcement is much easier with registered rights. It should then rank its markets by sales and by the risk of copying, so that limited money goes where the harm would be greatest. For monitoring, it can use a trade mark watch service for new applications, ask distributors and sales staff to report copies and send photos, and check online marketplaces and social media regularly. Each report should be logged with evidence, such as photos, purchases and dates. When a likely infringement is found, the firm should take legal advice and decide whether action is worth the cost, using a simple scale: small or distant problems may need only monitoring, while copies in key markets need prompt action. The first step is usually a formal letter, then negotiation, which may end in the copier stopping or taking a licence. Takedown requests can deal quickly with online sellers. Court action should be kept for serious cases. The firm should review results each year and adjust its budget.
markingPoints: Registers rights in key markets first
Prioritises markets by sales and risk
Uses watch services, staff, distributors and online checks
Logs evidence and weighs cost against harm
Escalates from letters and negotiation to court only when justified

essays.stem: Explain how IP should be managed at each stage of a new product development project, from the first idea to the launch.
essays.modelAnswer: At the idea stage, the team should record ideas with dates and names in a secure system and keep them confidential. Before spending much money, the team should search existing patents, designs and trade marks to see whether the idea is new and whether others' rights could block it. During design and development, staff should keep dated records, and any contractors, suppliers or partners should sign confidentiality agreements and contracts that say who owns the results. The IP officer should review progress at set points and decide what to protect and how: a patent for a new technical feature, a design registration for the look, and secrecy for the know-how. Applications should be filed before any public showing, testing with outside users or trade fair. At the branding stage, the name and logo should be cleared and registered in the launch markets. Before launch, the team should check that all third-party material, such as software or images, is licensed. After launch, the firm should monitor for copies, keep its registrations in force and record the product's IP in the register.
markingPoints: Records ideas and keeps them confidential from the start
Early searches for novelty and others' rights
Agreements with contractors and partners on confidentiality and ownership
Decides and files protection before public disclosure
Clears the brand, checks licences, monitors after launch

essays.stem: Compare the cost, market and income approaches to valuing IP, and recommend which suits a well-known brand that the owner plans to license.
essays.modelAnswer: The cost approach values IP by what it cost to create, or what it would cost to replace. It uses figures that are easy to find, but cost often has little link to value: a brand that cost little may earn a great deal. The market approach values IP by looking at prices paid for similar rights in sales or licences. It reflects what buyers actually pay, but IP is often unique and comparable deals are rarely public, especially in Jamaica. The income approach values IP by the future earnings it is expected to bring in, discounted to today's value. One form, relief from royalty, estimates the royalties the owner saves by not having to license the brand from someone else. This approach links value directly to earnings, but it depends on forecasts and on choosing a suitable royalty rate and discount rate, which can be argued over. For a well-known brand that will be licensed, I recommend the income approach, using relief from royalty, because licence fees are themselves royalties and the valuation then speaks directly to the negotiation. Market evidence of royalty rates should be used to support the rate chosen.
markingPoints: Cost approach and its weakness
Market approach and its limits
Income approach, including relief from royalty
Notes reliance on forecasts and rates
Justified recommendation for a licensed brand

essays.stem: A Kingston technology start-up expects an investor to carry out due diligence in three months. Describe how the firm should prepare its IP for this review.
essays.modelAnswer: The firm should first list all its IP: software code, the app name and logo, domain names, designs, data, know-how and any patents applied for. For each item, it should confirm and document ownership. This means checking that founders have formally assigned to the company any IP they created before it was set up, and that staff and freelancers have contracts that transfer their work to the company. Any gaps should be fixed now with written assignments. The firm should check that registrations and renewals are up to date and in the company's name, not a founder's. It should list all third-party software and open-source code used and confirm the licence terms are being met, as some licences can affect how the product may be sold. It should gather all licences it has granted or received, and any disputes or warnings. It should then prepare a clear IP schedule and a secure data room with the supporting documents. Finally, it should be ready to explain how its IP strategy supports the business plan, because investors want to see that the IP is protected and will produce income.
markingPoints: Lists all IP assets
Confirms ownership, with assignments from founders, staff and freelancers
Checks registrations are current and in the company's name
Reviews third-party and open-source licences and any disputes
Prepares an organised schedule, data room and strategy explanation

essays.stem: Describe how a manager should carry out a yearly review of a firm's IP portfolio to control costs and find new opportunities for growth.
essays.modelAnswer: The manager would start with the IP register and check that it is complete and up to date. For each right, she would note what it covers, where it is registered, its renewal date and cost, and which products and income it supports. She would meet the heads of sales, marketing and product development to confirm which products and markets matter now and in the next few years. Rights that support current or planned products in key markets would be kept and renewed. Rights that no longer support any plan would be considered for sale, licensing or being allowed to lapse, which saves renewal fees. She would also look for gaps, such as new products or markets without protection, and for chances to earn more, such as licensing a mark in a market the firm will not enter, or using a technology in another industry. She would review any infringements and licences, including whether licensees are paying correctly. The results would go into a short report to the board, with costs, savings, risks and recommended actions, and the register would be updated.
markingPoints: Uses an up-to-date register with costs and links to income
Consults business leaders on current and future plans
Decides to keep, sell, license or drop each right
Finds gaps and new income opportunities
Reports to the board and updates the register

essays.stem: Justify to the board of a medium-sized manufacturer why it should give a named manager responsibility and a yearly budget for IP management, and suggest how it should measure the results.
essays.modelAnswer: Much of the firm's value now lies in its brands, designs, product formulas and know-how, not just its machines. At present, IP is handled only when a problem arises, so renewals are missed, new products are launched without checks and nobody is sure what the firm owns. A named manager would make one person accountable for keeping the register, meeting deadlines and advising on protection before launches. A yearly budget would allow planned filings, watch services and legal advice, which cost far less than disputes, lost marks or relaunching a product under a new name. Clear ownership of IP would also make the firm more attractive to lenders, investors and licensing partners, and could bring in new income from licences. To measure results, the board should receive a quarterly report showing the share of revenue from protected products, licensing income, IP spending against budget, renewals met on time, new rights filed, and infringements found and resolved. It should also track whether each new product passed IP checks before launch. These measures show whether the spending is protecting value and helping the firm grow.
markingPoints: Explains the value of IP and the problems of no clear ownership
Benefits of one accountable manager
Budget compared with the cost of disputes and loss
Links to finance, investors and licensing income
Suitable measures reported to the board

practical1.title: Prepare an IP strategy and protection budget for an export launch
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a case pack for a made-up Jamaican firm (for example a hot sauce maker, a skincare brand or a furniture designer) that plans to launch a new product line in three export markets over two years. The pack includes the business plan summary, a list of the firm's current IP, sample search results showing some similar marks, and a table of registration and legal costs. As a group, produce: a two-page IP strategy linked to the business goals; a registration plan and timeline (Gantt chart) showing what will be protected, where and when, filed before launch; a protection budget in a spreadsheet with totals by year and by market; and an IP risk register with at least six risks, their rating and action. Present the strategy to the assessor, acting as the board, in ten minutes. Give each member a named role: strategy lead (writes the strategy and chairs the presentation), registration planner (builds the timeline), budget officer (builds and checks the spreadsheet), risk officer (builds the risk register), and research officer (reviews the search results and market information). In a group of four, the strategy lead also does the research. Every member presents their part. Photograph or screenshot each stage.
materials: Case pack from the assessor, including the cost table and search results
Computers with spreadsheet, word-processing and presentation software
photos: The group's flipchart map of the firm's IP and target markets
The registration timeline (Gantt chart) on screen
The protection budget spreadsheet showing totals and formulas
The group presenting to the assessor as the board
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Strategy is clearly linked to the firm's export goals
Protection is filed before launch in each market and matches each asset
Budget figures are calculated correctly and add up
Risks are realistic, rated and have actions
Answered the board's questions with sound reasons
Kept the case information confidential and worked respectfully
safety: Use only the made-up case and do not copy real firms' brands
Keep the case pack and outputs confidential to the group and the assessor
Check spreadsheet formulas twice before presenting figures
Share the workload fairly and take short screen breaks

practical2.title: Appraise ways to commercialise a patented invention and recommend one
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a case pack for a made-up Jamaican firm that holds a patent on a new product (for example a solar crop dryer, a water-saving irrigation valve or a hurricane shutter clip). The pack includes the firm's finances, market estimates, and offers or estimates for four options: making the product itself, licensing it, selling the patent, and a joint venture. As a group, produce: a spreadsheet comparing the five-year expected income, costs and net result of each option; a scoring table that rates each option against agreed criteria (income, risk, control, capital needed and growth); a three-page recommendation report with the reasons, the main risks and the key terms the firm should seek; and a short presentation to the firm's owners. Give each member a named role: project lead (keeps time and writes the report's summary and recommendation), financial analyst (builds the spreadsheet), risk analyst (assesses the risks of each option), terms adviser (lists the key licence or deal terms), and presenter (prepares the slides; every member presents a part). In a group of four, the project lead also prepares the slides. Photograph or screenshot each stage.
materials: Case pack from the assessor, including the option figures
Computers with spreadsheet, word-processing and presentation software
photos: The flipchart list of options and the criteria agreed
The spreadsheet comparing the options, with formulas shown
The list of key terms for the chosen option
The group presenting to the owners
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Calculated each option's five-year result correctly
Compared the options against clear, sensible criteria
Identified the main risks of each option and how to manage them
Made a recommendation that follows from the analysis
Presented their part clearly and answered questions
Respected teammates' views and shared the work fairly
safety: Use only the made-up case figures and names
Keep the case pack and analysis confidential
Check calculations twice before they go into the report
Speak respectfully, let every member contribute and take short screen breaks
